messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Luther, a 61‑year‑old bus driver who has spent more than three decades hauling passengers along the downtown corridor, first encountered the violence that would come to haunt him during a protest in his early twenties. While marching with a coalition of civil‑rights activists, he was seized by a paramilitary squad and taken to a clandestine facility where he endured hours of interrogation and physical torment. The memory of the stony walls, the metallic taste of blood on his lips, and the crackling of the electric shocks still flash in his mind in flashes of hyper‑clarity, yet many other moments remain shrouded, as if the darkness of the cell had erased them. He has never told a friend about the night he was left on a concrete slab, his throat raw, his body trembling; the experience became a fragmentary, terror‑laden recollection that feels both too vivid and disturbingly incomplete. Because the terror on recall is so intense, Luther finds his nights suffused with vigilance. He wakes repeatedly, heart hammering, and listens for the faintest creak of a door or the distant rumble of a truck, convinced a new threat is lurking just beyond his bedroom window. Whenever the sudden jolt of an alarm clock or the hiss of the kitchen stove triggers a flashback, his body reacts with a surge of adrenaline, his muscles tightening, his breath shallow. In these moments, the memory of his own helplessness in that cell resurfaces, making the present feel as if the walls of the interrogation room had collapsed around him. The terror he experiences at night is not a passive echo; it feeds back into the way he perceives the present, making every ordinary sound feel like a potential harbinger of the violence that once defined his life. The guilt that gnaws at Luther’s mind compounds his sense of danger. He believes he should have fought harder, that his inaction was a sign of weakness, and that he failed to protect not only himself but also the comrades he shared the protest with. These negative appraisals magnify the threat he feels in the dark; when he thinks of how he could have intervened, his anxiety spikes, and the very thought of walking into the night triggers a cascade of worry. At the same time, each nocturnal episode of alarm and panic reinforces his belief that he is inherently weak, that he cannot command his body to stay calm. In this way, the fear he experiences at night does not simply mirror his memory; it becomes a self‑reinforcing echo that deepens his negative self‑evaluations. Luther’s perception of the incomplete picture of his trauma further entangles him in a cycle of self‑blame. The parts of the event that remain blank compel him to fill the gaps with the narrative of a failed protector, thereby strengthening his inaction guilt. As he reconstructs those missing moments, the sense that he was powerless or that he could not have done more takes root, shaping how he remembers the whole ordeal. The gaps, the missing details, and the terror that still grips him when he tries to recall the incident all feed back into the same loop of guilt and perceived weakness. For years, Luther has carried this loop into his daily life as a bus driver. When his route crosses the quiet, dimly lit avenues of the city at night, he finds himself unable to focus on the road, his hands trembling as he steers. The fear of a sudden threat at the wheel forces him to shorten his evening shift, which in turn causes tension at home with his wife, who worries that he is avoiding the night altogether. It is this mounting strain—on his job, his relationships, and his own sense of safety—that finally drives Luther to seek help. He hopes that by confronting the memories he keeps shivering from, he can quiet the night‑time vigilance and regain the confidence he once believed he lacked, and he fears that without intervention, the cycle will only tighten, robbing him of more moments with his family and his livelihood.
